title: Chapter 2: Return to the City - Boyhood Years
primary_topics: Chapter 2 covers the post-war Manila boyhood (1945-1954): the family's return from Candaba to Sampaloc, the briefly attempted bootblack work, and then the formative newsboy years on Cataluña Street that supply both the income to support his studies and the diary-line ('Today I'm just a newsboy. Someday, I'll be president of the Manila Times') that will be redeemed decades later when he becomes president of the Philippine Daily Inquirer.

Working-student arithmetic: 10/15-centavo daily papers, 2-3 centavos commission per copy, a wooden *cariton* (cart) built to carry more, a credit system invented to outrun the other boys to customers' doors -- Sampaloc as the practical school of enterprise, with Manila Times as the dominant daily, Manila Chronicle/Philippine Herald/Bulletin as competitors, and Evening News/Daily Mirror as afternoon papers.

Schooling under hardship: Juan Luna Elementary School (Grade IV with strict disciplinarian Mrs. Isabel Fajardo), then Victorino Mapa High School (1950-1954) -- one of four Manila public high schools named after Filipino jurists (Arellano, Araullo, Mapa, Torres), with 6,000+ students; CJP graduating 'Honorable Mention' in a class of about 1,000, top ten -- a notable alumni roster including Arturo M. Tolentino (later Senate President / 9th VP), Washington SyCip (SGV co-founder), and Jose Melo (future SC justice).

The four scholarships and the religious-illiteracy moment: the UP full scholarship CJP qualified for but could not take because his father could not afford the 15-centavo daily bus fare to Diliman; the UST scholarship interview that turned on the Holy Trinity ('How many persons in one God?') and that CJP failed by answering 'Jesus, Mary and Joseph' -- and FEU as the walking-distance fallback that would become the pivot of his life.

The father's wish: Artemio Sr. discovering 'chemical engineer' in his son's high-school yearbook 'Ambition' entry and asking, gravely, that the son who carried his name pursue law instead -- 'so he would truly live in me.' CJP agreed with the condition that he could revert to engineering after the two-year Associate in Arts. Temi died before the two years were over, and CJP completed law and dropped the 'Jr.' from his name in his father's honor.

stances.claim: Poverty was not just hardship but pedagogy -- the newsboy years taught the discipline, enterprise, and arithmetic that would define CJP's professional habits. Building a *cariton*, inventing a credit system to beat other boys, and tracking commissions to the centavo were the first decisive form of his agency.
stances.rhetorical_move: poverty-as-school framing; hardship reread as competence-formation

stances.claim: The diary line 'Today I am just a newsboy. Someday I'll be president of the Manila Times' is treated by the biography as not childhood bravado but prophecy -- fulfilled in March 1991 at PDI and ratified again via the Sunday column from 2011. The chapter frames it as the first articulation of CJP's later pattern of aim-and-arrival.

Catholic religious illiteracy at the UST interview -- answering 'Jesus, Mary and Joseph' to 'name the three persons in one God' -- was not merely a missed scholarship but the providential turn. The UST failure pushed CJP to FEU, where Fr. Nolan and the SCA awaited; the loss was a redirection.

The father's wish -- that the son who carried his name pursue law because 'I was his last chance to fulfil his frustrated ambition' -- is the binding promise that overrode CJP's preference for chemical engineering. Combined with Temi's early death, it became an inheritance that could not be returned: 'so he would truly live in me.'
stances.rhetorical_move: filial-vow framing; inherited vocation as constraint and gift

stances.claim: Discipline as gift from named hands: Mrs. Isabel Fajardo's ruler at Juan Luna and Dean Salonga's grade-monitoring at FEU (next chapter) form a chain of named mentors whose specific habits CJP credits for the orderliness of his later life -- a teacher-by-teacher genealogy rather than abstract self-discipline.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 follows the post-war family return from Candaba to Sampaloc, Manila, and the formation of CJP's working-student identity from roughly age 9 to 18. After a brief stint as a bootblack, Dayunior pursued newspaper-selling on Cataluña Street with the enterprise that would mark his whole life: building a wooden *cariton* to carry more copies, instituting a credit-and-collect system to beat other boys to the doors, and tracking the 2- or 3-centavo commissions on the 10- or 15-centavo dailies (Manila Times, Manila Chronicle, Philippine Herald, Manila Bulletin in the mornings; Evening News, Daily Mirror in the afternoons). Through years of sleeping on the sidewalk near the news dealer's apartment to get first crack at delivery trucks -- and one near-fatal jeepney fall on España and Lerma Streets that a 6x6 military truck nearly turned terminal -- he supplied his own school money, supported his family in small ways, and built the *alkansya* he would keep into professional life as a trophy. In a diary on the cold pavement he wrote 'Today I am just a newsboy. Someday, I will be president of the Manila Times' -- a line redeemed in March 1991 when he became president of the Philippine Daily Inquirer, and again in 2011 when Marixi Prieto invited him back as a regular Sunday columnist; he later donated an entire year's professional fee to the Inquirer Newsboys Foundation. Schooling alternated with the route: Juan Luna Elementary School (where Grade IV's strict Mrs. Isabel Fajardo and her ruler 'could be credited with my being disciplined the rest of my life'), then Victorino Mapa High School from 1950 to 1954 -- one of four Manila public high schools named after Filipino jurists (Arellano, Araullo, Mapa, Torres), the largest with over 6,000 students, with classmates like future Senate President / 9th VP Arturo M. Tolentino, SGV co-founder Washington SyCip, and future SC justice and Comelec chair Jose Melo -- where Dayunior graduated Honorable Mention in the top 10 of about 1,000 seniors. He earned a UP full scholarship but could not afford the 15-centavo daily bus fare to Diliman; he tried for a UST scholarship but lost it to the third Holy Trinity question, replying 'Jesus, Mary and Joseph' to the old Dominican priest. FEU sat five minutes and two streets away from Cataluña, the walking-distance fallback that would become the pivot of his life. The chapter closes with his father's discovery of 'chemical engineer' in the yearbook 'Ambition' entry and the gravely-spoken request: that the son who carried Artemio Sr.'s name pursue law instead -- 'so he would truly live in me.' Dayunior agreed with a two-year escape clause, not knowing that Temi would die during his first pre-law year and that the filial vow would become irrevocable.
